title: JESUS ASKED FOR THE CUP TO PASS—THEN HE CHOSE THE CROSS
paragraphs:
JESUS ASKED FOR THE CUP TO PASS—THEN HE CHOSE THE CROSS
Gethsemane reveals something terrifyingly beautiful: Jesus did not walk toward Calvary because suffering was easy. He walked toward Calvary because saving sinners was the Father’s will—and He surrendered completely.
There is a prayer Jesus prayed that becomes almost unbearable when you understand what He knew was coming.
It was not spoken before a cheering crowd.
There were no multitudes pressing around Him for healing.
No children running toward Him.
No astonished disciples celebrating another miracle.
It was dark.
The hour was late.
And somewhere beneath the ancient olive trees of Gethsemane, Jesus Christ fell on His face before His Father.
Within hours, Judas would arrive.
The arrest would begin.
The disciples would scatter.
Peter would deny Him.
False witnesses would speak.
Soldiers would mock Him.
His body would be scourged.
Thorns would be pressed upon His head.
Nails would tear through flesh.
And eventually the sinless Son of God would hang upon a Roman cross.
Jesus knew.
That changes everything about what He prayed next.
Matthew records His words:
“Πάτερ μου, εἰ δυνατόν ἐστιν, παρελθάτω ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο· πλὴν οὐχ ὡς ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλ’ ὡς σύ.”
Pater mou, ei dynaton estin, parelthatō ap’ emou to potērion touto; plēn ouch hōs egō thelō all’ hōs sy.
“My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will.”
—Matthew 26:39
Read it again.
Slowly.
Jesus asked for the cup to pass.
And then came the words upon which the road to Calvary continued:
“Not as I will, but as You will.”
That is Gethsemane.
Not pretending the suffering was painless.
Not denying the horror ahead.
Not performing some emotionless version of spirituality in which obedience means you never tremble.
Jesus brought the agony into the presence of His Father...
and surrendered.
Mark gives us another detail so intimate that the Gospel preserves the Aramaic word Jesus used:
Ἀββᾶ — Abba.
“Abba, Father.”
The Greek text reads:
“Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ, πάντα δυνατά σοι· παρένεγκε τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ· ἀλλ’ οὐ τί ἐγὼ θέλω ἀλλὰ τί σύ.”
“Abba, Father, all things are possible for You. Take this cup away from Me; nevertheless, not what I will, but what You will.”
—Mark 14:36
Abba is Aramaic for “father.”
Do not reduce it to sentimental baby talk.
The beauty is already powerful enough without exaggerating it.
Jesus is speaking to His Father in intimacy, trust, and obedience while facing an anguish almost beyond our comprehension.
And perhaps someone reading this understands a tiny shadow of that kind of prayer.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Father, please don't let this happen.”
“Please save my marriage.”
“Please heal her.”
“Please bring him home.”
“Please don't let me lose this.”
“Please open this door.”
“Please make the diagnosis different.”
“Please take this pain away.”
“Please change their heart.”
“Please change my circumstances.”
And sometimes Christians become ashamed of prayers like that.
We imagine mature faith means never admitting what we desperately want.
Then Gethsemane destroys that illusion.
Jesus asked.
He expressed His desire honestly.
There was no unbelief in His honesty.
There was no rebellion in His anguish.
The sinless Christ prayed, in essence, “If it is possible, let this cup pass.”
But He did not stop there.
That is where surrender begins.
“Nevertheless...”
Perhaps that is one of the most costly words ever prayed.
Father, this is what I want...
nevertheless.
Father, this hurts...
nevertheless.
Father, I do not desire this suffering...
nevertheless.
Father, if there is another way...
nevertheless.
Not my will above Yours.
Not my comfort above Your purpose.
Not escape at the price of obedience.
Your will.
That does not mean Christians should call every tragedy “God's will,” refuse medical treatment, remain in abuse, or passively accept evil.
Biblical surrender is not fatalism.
It is entrusting ourselves to the wisdom and authority of God while obeying what He has revealed.
And no one embodied that obedience more perfectly than Jesus Christ.
There is another reason the word cup matters.

Throughout Scripture, a cup can symbolize what God appoints someone to receive, and in sobering passages it becomes imagery associated with divine judgment. Isaiah speaks of “the cup of His fury” and “the cup of trembling.” Jeremiah describes the nations receiving the wine cup of God's wrath. The prophets repeatedly use this frightening picture.
So when Jesus speaks of τὸ ποτήριον — to potērion — “the cup,” we should not reduce Gethsemane merely to fear of physical pain.
Crucifixion would indeed be horrific.
But the Gospel takes us deeper.
At the cross, Christ would accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Scripture says:
“He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.”
—2 Corinthians 5:21
Peter writes that Christ “bore our sins in His own body on the tree.”
Paul says Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, “having become a curse for us.”
Isaiah, centuries before Calvary, spoke prophetically of the Servant who would be “wounded for our transgressions” and “bruised for our iniquities.”
This is why Gethsemane cannot be separated from the Gospel.
Jesus was not an unfortunate victim trapped by circumstances.
He had repeatedly told His disciples what was coming.
He knew Jerusalem awaited Him.
He knew betrayal awaited Him.
He knew the cross awaited Him.
And still He went.
The cup did not pass.
Jesus drank it.
The cup that did not pass from Christ is connected to the mercy offered to sinners like us.
The judgment our sins deserve.
The condemnation we could never remove.
The debt we could never repay.
Christ went willingly toward the cross.
Not because humanity was innocent.
Because humanity was guilty.
Not because we had finally become lovable enough.
Because God loved sinners who could never rescue themselves.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
We prefer religions where respectable people climb upward toward God.
The Gospel announces something completely different.
God came down for sinners.
For adulterers.
For liars.
For hypocrites.
For addicts.
For the religiously proud.
For the sexually broken.
For people carrying secrets nobody knows.
For churchgoers who know exactly how to raise their hands during worship while quietly losing their souls.
For the person reading this who has deleted messages so nobody would discover the truth.
For the person who keeps promising God, “This is the last time.”
For the woman smiling in photographs while crying when nobody is watching.
For the man everyone thinks is strong who is spiritually exhausted.
For the believer wondering whether God could possibly forgive what happened again last night.
Gethsemane whispers something before Calvary shouts it:
Jesus knew exactly what saving sinners would cost Him...and He kept walking.
That does not make sin small.
It makes grace astonishing.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Look at Gethsemane.
Look at Calvary.
Sin matters so profoundly that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And yet sinners matter so profoundly to God that the Son willingly gave Himself.
That is why the Gospel never says, “Stay exactly as you are.”
Jesus calls sinners to repent.
To turn.
To believe.
To leave darkness.
To come into the light.
Grace does not give sin permission to keep destroying you.
Grace breaks sin's claim over the person who belongs to Christ.
Maybe that is why this story makes us uncomfortable.
We want Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Heaven without surrender.
Grace without transformation.
Resurrection without a cross.
We want Christianity to fit around the life we have already decided to live.
Then Jesus falls upon His face in Gethsemane and prays:
“Not what I will, but what You will.”
Suddenly the question becomes personal.
What have you refused to surrender?
Not your neighbor.
Not your spouse.
Not that politician.
Not the hypocrite at church.
You.
What is the thing you keep protecting from the lordship of Jesus?
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Him?
The pornography nobody knows about?
The bitterness you have rehearsed so long that it feels like part of your identity?
The secret conversation?
The pride?
The addiction?
The money?
The unforgiveness?
The need to control everything?
The version of Christianity where Jesus may advise you but never command you?
We often pray, “Lord, change my circumstances.”
Gethsemane teaches us to add:
“Lord, even when You do not change my circumstances the way I want, make my heart obedient to You.”
That prayer is frightening.
Because surrender costs something.
Jesus never disguised that.
“If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me.”
Christianity was never supposed to be Jesus decorating the life of our choosing.
It is death and resurrection.
The old life surrendered.
A new life received.
And maybe tonight your Gethsemane is not a garden.
Maybe it is your bedroom floor.
Your parked car.
A hospital corridor.
A divorce lawyer's office.
An unanswered message.
An empty chair at the table.
A bank account you are afraid to open.
A temptation you are exhausted from fighting.
A prayer you have prayed for five years without seeing the answer you wanted.
Listen carefully.
Gethsemane does not promise that every cup you ask God to remove will be removed.
It gives us something deeper.
It shows us a Savior who understands anguish.
A Savior who prayed through sorrow.
A Savior who obeyed through suffering.
A Savior who can be trusted when obedience hurts.
And the story did not end in the garden.
Nor did it end at the cross.
Friday came.
The nails came.
The darkness came.
The tomb came.
But Sunday came too.
Jesus Christ rose.
The One who surrendered Himself unto death defeated death.
The crucified Christ became the risen Christ.
And because He lives, repentance is not the funeral of hope.
It is the doorway into life.
Your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Your worst night does not have to become your identity.
Your failure does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is what we mean when we say:
Not from scandal to pretending it never happened.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to religious image management.
From scandal...
through repentance...
into grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you arrived at this article thinking about Christ's surrender.
Maybe somewhere along the way you realized God was confronting yours.
If something hidden has been exposed in your heart, don't hide behind another scroll.
Be honest.
Or simply tell your story. Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person still fighting to follow Jesus.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them they are not walking alone.
There may come a night when “not my will, but Yours” becomes the prayer you need more than anything else.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow as well. We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Not because anyone can purchase God's favor.
You cannot.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It never will.
Salvation is God's gift of grace in Jesus Christ.
But Christians may freely support Gospel ministry from gratitude and a desire to help truth reach others.
Come to Christ.
Not to a page.
Not to a brand.
Not merely to a Christian community.
To Jesus.
If you have been running, repent and come home.
If you have been hiding, step into His light.
If you have been trying to clean yourself up before approaching Him, stop trying to become your own savior.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentant faith finds a Savior greater than their sin.
Gethsemane began with a cup Jesus asked to pass.
It continued with surrender.
It led to a cross.
The cross led to a tomb.
And the tomb became empty.
So when your own obedience becomes costly, remember the Savior beneath the olive trees.
Remember His face toward the ground.
Remember His prayer.
Remember His surrender.
Remember that He stood up afterward and kept walking toward those who had come to arrest Him.
And remember why.
He was going to the cross.
For sinners.
For redemption.
For grace.
For the glory of His Father.
The cup did not pass from Jesus—but because He drank it, sinners who deserve judgment can receive mercy through Him.
